paras: The attempted lynching of Ben Lee took place on the night of June 12, 1903, when a crowd broke into the jail at Greenville, Illinois, to seize Lee, a Black prisoner accused of assaulting a white woman. Sheriff Floyd had driven Lee away hours earlier, and the mob found the jail empty. Newspapers across the country carried the story as 'a second attempt at lynching in Illinois within a week.'

Lee was charged with entering the house of Mary Larrabee, four miles east of Greenville, at one o'clock in the morning. The St. Louis Republic's Greenville correspondent named her 'Miss May Larrabee' and reported that her mother was in critical condition from the shock. Sheriff Floyd arrested Lee on the afternoon of June 12 while he was working on a farm south of town, and Lee protested his innocence. According to the Republic, Lee was then on parole from the Chester Penitentiary.

Crowds gathered as news of the arrest spread, and by evening, in the words of one dispatch, 'excitement soon was running at fever heat.' Warned that an attempt would be made to lynch the prisoner, the sheriff took Lee out of the jail about seven o'clock and drove him by buggy to Carlyle. At about 10:30 p.m. a 'crowd of citizens' went to the Bond County jail, broke in the doors and found the prisoner gone. The Republic reported that the mob did not disperse until early the next morning, after the men had seen for themselves that Lee was not inside, and that the sheriff returned from Carlyle at three o'clock.

Lee was to be held at the Chester Penitentiary, and the Republic expected an indictment from the September grand jury. No arrests of members of the mob were reported. On March 24, 1904, a Greenville dispatch reported that Lee had pleaded guilty and been sentenced to life in the penitentiary, having been kept at Chester since his arrest 'to prevent lynching.' That brief dated the assault to 'last fall', which does not match the June 1903 reports.

The episode reached readers mainly through a Record-Herald dispatch from Greenville, relayed from Chicago and printed on June 13 and 14 in papers from Washington and New York to Salt Lake City and Savannah. Its headlines stressed the mob's failure, as in 'LYNCHING FRUSTRATED', 'ILLINOIS LYNCHERS FOILED' and 'AVOIDED A LYNCHING', and the text credited 'the vigilance of the authorities.' Southern weeklies in Tennessee, Arkansas and Mississippi reprinted the dispatch a week later under 'WOULD-BE LYNCHERS FOILED.'

Some Southern dailies used the story to point at Illinois. The Raleigh News and Observer headed it 'JUDGE LYNCH IN ILLINOIS' with the subhead 'The Only Thing That Saved the Negro Was, He Wasn't There.' The Richmond Times Dispatch gave it one line among its editorial paragraphs, saying the attempt 'failed only because the negro was fleet of foot' and calling the charge the 'usual crime.' The St. Louis Republic, closer to the scene, sent its own report describing a 'mob of angry citizens' bent on 'summary punishment' and calling the accuser 'the outraged girl.' All of the coverage found came from white newspapers, which named Lee's race but not the mob's.

Every news report says the sheriff removed Lee before the mob arrived, but the Richmond Times Dispatch, without a source, said he escaped because he was 'fleet of foot.' The accuser is 'Mary Larrabee' in the wire report and the 1904 sentencing brief but 'Miss May Larrabee' in the Republic.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Ben Lee
bases: A crowd broke into the Greenville jail to seize Ben Lee for lynching, but he had been removed beforehand, so this is an attempted lynching (A1, A6, A10).

A 'crowd of citizens' broke the jail doors to lynch Lee on an accusation of assault, but he had already been taken away and was not harmed (A1, A10); he was later sentenced in court (A17), so no killing occurred.

The Record-Herald dispatch (A1, A10) and the St. Louis Republic's own Greenville correspondent (A6, A7) independently agree that a mob sought Lee at the Bond County jail after the sheriff had removed him; only a Richmond editorial quip (A8) says he escaped on foot.

framing.detail: Daily papers ran the Record-Herald dispatch under headlines such as 'LYNCHING FRUSTRATED', 'ILLINOIS LYNCHERS FOILED' and 'AVOIDED A LYNCHING', crediting 'the vigilance of the authorities'.
The St. Louis Republic's correspondent wrote of a 'mob of angry citizens' bent on 'summary punishment' and called the accuser's daughter 'the outraged girl', presenting the accusation as fact.

The Richmond Times Dispatch treated the attempt as a quip about Illinois and the 'usual crime'; the Raleigh News & Observer headed it 'JUDGE LYNCH IN ILLINOIS. The Only Thing That Saved the Negro Was, He Wasn't There.'
